records.requirements: Site preparation methods must be selected according to site conditions; invasive species management, erosion control, water quality protection, soil protection, and compliance with applicable laws and regulations are required

records.name: Upland Wildlife Habitat Management
records.problem: Degraded wildlife habitat, habitat fragmentation, lack of shelter, cover, food resources, or habitat connectivity for wildlife
records.strategies: Vegetation establishment for shelter, food, and movement; structural measures to provide shelter, food, or movement; vegetation management to sustain habitat conditions over tim
records.eligibility: Applies to land where there is an objective to conserve a wildlife species, guild, suite, or ecosystem, and where habitat can support the target species
records.requirements: Requires habitat evaluation to identify limiting factors; use of adapted, high-quality plant species; optimized site preparation and planting methods; control of invasive and noxious species; restriction of grazing, haying, and equipment use during critical wildlife periods

records.name: Vegetated Treatment Area
records.problem: Nutrient runoff, contaminated agricultural runoff, degraded surface water quality, pathogen transport, agricultural wastewater discharge
records.strategies: Permanent vegetation used to treat agricultural wastewater; may include grasses, legumes, and other forbs adapted to site conditions; wastewater applied as sheet flow across a vegetated area for nutrient and contaminant removal
records.eligibility: Applies where a vegetated treatment area can be constructed and maintained to treat contaminated runoff from feedlots, feed storage areas, compost areas, manure storage areas, barnyards, livestock holding areas, or agricultural process wastewater; must be part of an agricultural waste management system
records.requirements: Requires permanent vegetation; exclusion of livestock; sheet-flow distribution; treatment area sized based on runoff and nutrient balances; uncontaminated water diverted when possible; vegetation selected to tolerate wet or submerged conditions; subsurface drainage not allowed within the VTA

records.name: Vegetative Barrier
records.problem: Sheet and rill erosion, ephemeral gully erosion, sediment transport to surface waters
records.strategies: Permanent strips of stiff, dense vegetation established along contours or across concentrated flow areas; vegetation must be adapted to local soil and climate conditions, long-lived, manageable, and capable of maintaining dense, upright stems; may be established from seed or vegetative material
records.eligibility: Applies to all land uses where sheet and rill erosion or ephemeral gully erosion are resource concerns
records.requirements: Vegetation must meet minimum density and stiffness requirements; invasive and noxious species are prohibited; barriers must be established and maintained as dense vegetative strips; site preparation, seeding, planting, weed control, and maintenance are required

records.name: Wetland Creation
records.problem: Frequent flooding, loss of wetland habitat, poor water quality, loss of native wetland vegetation, conversion of uplands to wetland conditions due to changing hydrology
records.strategies: Creation of a wetland on a site that was historically not a wetland; establishment of wetland hydrology through shallow inundation or soil saturation; may include wetland vegetation established by natural colonization, seeding, or planting; may include native wetland plant communities, herbaceous vegetation, shrubs, and trees adapted to anaerobic conditions
records.eligibility: Applies to all NRCS land uses where wetland hydrology can be established on a site that was historically not a wetland
records.requirements: Wetland hydrology must be established and maintained; existing surface or subsurface drains may need to be removed, plugged, relocated, or made inoperable; vegetation must be adapted to wetland conditions; invasive species should be controlled; water rights must be adequate where applicable

records.name: Wetland Enhancement
records.problem: Degraded wetlands, loss of wetland habitat, altered hydrology, invasive species, reduced native wetland vegetation, reduced fish and wildlife habitat
records.strategies: Enhancement of existing wetlands through hydrology management, hydric soil improvements, vegetation enhancement, invasive species removal, seeding or planting desired wetland species, water control structures, microtopography or macrotopography modifications, and habitat improvements
records.eligibility: Applies to degraded or non-degraded wetland sites with hydric soils where the objective is to enhance selected wetland functions beyond original natural conditions
records.requirements: Must occur on an existing wetland with hydric soils; enhancement objectives must be clearly defined; invasive and noxious species must be controlled; preference given to native wetland plants and local genetic material; hydrology, soils, vegetation, and habitat conditions must support the enhancement objectives

records.name: Wetland Restoration
records.problem: Loss of wetlands, altered hydrology, drainage of wetlands, wetland degradation, loss of wetland habitat, reduced water quality, changes in wetland vegetation
records.strategies: Re-establishment of wetland hydrology, topography, and substrate to approximate historic wetland conditions; may include removal of fill, breaking or removing drainage tile, replacing perforated tile with solid tile, breaching berms or levees, filling pits or ponds, grading to restore microtopography, and installing water control structures
records.eligibility: Applies where a naturally occurring wetland historically existed but has been altered by drainage, filling, excavation, leveling, ditches, tile drainage, reservoirs, levees, diversions, or other disturbances, and the objective is to restore pre-disturbance wetland conditions
records.requirements: Restoration must target the original hydrogeomorphic class and vegetative modifier of the historic wetland; hydrology, water source, inundation patterns, and hydrologic losses should be restored as closely as practicable to historic conditions; hazardous material sites are not eligible

records.name: Wetland Wildlife Habitat Management
records.problem: Loss of wetland habitat, reduced habitat quality for wetland-dependent wildlife, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, lack of nesting, feeding, or cover habitat
records.strategies: Management of wetland habitat through native plant establishment, invasive species control, water level management, vegetative buffers, artificial nesting structures, snags, logs, tree trunks, and other habitat features that support wetland-dependent wildlif
records.eligibility: Applies on or adjacent to wetlands, rivers, lakes, and other water bodies where wetland-associated wildlife habitat can be managed; applies to natural wetlands and wetlands that have been restored (CPS657), enhanced (CPS659), or created (CPS658)
records.requirements: Requires habitat evaluation to identify limiting factors; wildlife management objectives must be defined; native plants should be used whenever possible; invasive and noxious species ( e.g. Phragmites) must be controlled; habitat management must address identified limiting factors

records.name: Wildlife Habitat Planting
records.problem: Degraded wildlife habitat, low plant diversity, poor pollinator habitat, lack of food and cover for wildlife, conversion of cropland or pastureland to habitat
records.strategies: Establishment of wildlife habitat through planting herbaceous vegetation and/or shrubs; may include native grasses, forbs, shrubs, pollinator habitat plantings, and plant communities designed to resemble historic native vegetation
records.eligibility: Applies to all lands where inadequate wildlife habitat is identified as a primary resource concern and habitat evaluations indicate a benefit from altering existing vegetation
records.requirements: Use only noninvasive species adapted to the site; native plant materials should be used when suitable and available; invasive and noxious species risks must be addressed; planting design must meet habitat objectives for target wildlife species or guilds; establishment and maintenance activities are required throughout the practice lifespan

records.name: Windbreak/Shelterbelt Establishment and Renovation
records.problem: Wind erosion, wind damage to plants, ponding and flooding associated with snow accumulation, poor moisture management, livestock exposure to wind and heat, air quality concerns
records.strategies: Single or multiple rows of trees and/or shrubs established, enhanced, or renovated in linear or curvilinear configurations
records.eligibility: Applies on all lands except forest land where rows of woody plants are desired and suited for the intended purpose; also applies to existing windbreaks requiring renovation
records.requirements: Trees and shrubs must be suitable for the intended purpose and site conditions; windbreaks must be designed to achieve the intended function

records.name: Woody Residue Treatment
records.problem: Excess woody debris, hazardous fuel accumulation, insect and disease risks, restricted access for management activities, reduced forage access, impaired regeneration of plant communities
records.strategies: Treatment of residual woody material through chipping, mastication, crushing, compacting, lop and scatter, piling, burning, or offsite removal; adequate woody material is retained to support nutrient cycling, soil protection, and soil organic matter
records.eligibility: Applies on all lands except active cropland where woody residue requires treatment
records.requirements: Treatment methods must be selected based on the condition, volume, and extent of woody residue; minimize impacts to residual vegetation and soils; retain sufficient woody material to maintain nutrient and organic matter cycling, protect soil surface, and minimize soil compaction; burning activities must comply with prescribed burning and air quality requirements

records.name: Herbaceous Weed Treatment
records.problem: Invasive, noxious, prohibited, or undesirable herbaceous plants; reduced forage quality; degraded wildlife habitat; erosion concerns; excessive fine fuels and wildfire hazard
records.strategies: Removal or control of herbaceous weeds using mechanical, chemical, biological, or integrated methods; may include mowing, manual removal, targeted grazing, herbicides, or spot-flaming
records.eligibility: Applies on all lands except active cropland where removal, reduction, or manipulation of herbaceous vegetation is desired
records.requirements: Treatments must achieve control of target species while protecting desired vegetation; weed prevention strategies should minimize soil disturbance and spread of weeds; post-treatment revegetation may be required; treatments must comply with herbicide labels and applicable regulations

records.name: Irrigation Field Ditch
records.problem: Inefficient irrigation water delivery, poor water distribution, water losses during irrigation
records.strategies: Permanent earthen irrigation ditch used to convey water from a water source to one or more irrigated fields; may include vegetative cover on ditch banks and associated water-control structures
records.eligibility: Applies where field ditches are needed as part of an irrigation water distribution system; limited to open channels and elevated earth ditches with capacities of 25 cubic feet per second or less
records.requirements: Water supply must be adequate for planned crops and irrigation methods; ditch capacity must meet irrigation demand; ditch must be constructed in suitable soils to minimize seepage and erosion; operation and maintenance are required to maintain function and vegetative cover

records.name: Structure for Water Control
records.problem: Poor water-level management, flooding, drainage issues, water table management needs, wetland hydrology restoration, tidal backflow, saltwater movement through drainage systems
records.strategies: Permanent water-control structures including flashboard risers, water level control structures, check dams, checks, head gates, pipe drop inlets, box inlets, tide gates, water management gates, culverts, chutes, and water measurement devices
records.eligibility: Applies where a permanent structure is needed as an integral part of a water management system to control water flow, water levels, drainage, irrigation, wetland hydrology, flooding, wildlife habitat, or tidal backflow
records.requirements: Structure must be part of a water control system; must comply with applicable permits and regulations; operation and maintenance plan required; disturbed areas require vegetative stabilization or mulching

records.name: Water and Sediment Control Basin (WASCOB)
records.problem: Gully erosion; sediment transport and deposition; excessive runoff; runoff and sediment damage to land and improvements
records.strategies: Earth embankment or combination ridge and channel constructed across the slope of a minor drainageway; basin may use an underground outlet, pipe drop structure, soil infiltration area, stable channel, or combination of outlet types; nonfarmed disturbed areas are vegetated with permanent native or noninvasive vegetation
records.eligibility: Applies where topography is generally irregular; gully erosion is a problem; other conservation practices typically control sheet and rill erosion; runoff and sediment damage land and works of improvement; and stable outlets are available
records.requirements: Basin must be planned, designed, and constructed to meet applicable regulations; installed as part of a conservation system; located to reduce erosion in a drainageway; designed with adequate runoff and sediment storage capacity; provided with a stable outlet; nonfarmed disturbed areas must be revegetated; an operation and maintenance plan is required

records.name: Contour Farming
records.problem: Sheet and rill erosion; sediment transport to surface waters; excess nutrients in surface waters; pesticide transport to surface waters; inefficient moisture management
records.strategies: Aligning ridges, furrows, and roughness formed by tillage, planting, and other operations at a grade near the contour to alter the velocity or direction of water flow
records.eligibility: Applies on sloping land where crops are grown; orchards, vineyards, and nut crops use CPS 331 instead
records.requirements: Row grades must be as near level as possible while allowing drainage; maximum row grade cannot exceed one-half of the up-and-down-hill slope used for conservation planning, with a maximum 4% row grade; positive row drainage of at least 0.2% is required where ponding is a concern; concentrated flow must be delivered to stable outlets; tillage and planting operations must be parallel to established contour baselines or other applicable contour markers

records.name: Contour Orchard and Other Perennial Crops
records.problem: Sheet and rill soil erosion; sediment transport to surface waters; poor water infiltration
records.strategies: Planting orchards, vineyards, or other perennial crops so field operations are performed on or near the contour; vegetative ground cover may be maintained in alleys, row furrows, terraces, and diversions to increase infiltration, reduce runoff, and control erosion
records.eligibility: Applies on sloping land where orchards, vineyards, or other perennial crops will be established in defined rows; does not apply to areas with evidence of mass soil movement or potential for landslides
records.requirements: Align row grades as close to the contour as possible; divert overland flow from adjacent sites; use temporary erosion control where sites are disturbed; provide positive row drainage of at least 0.2% where ponding is a concern; deliver runoff to stable outlets; maintain adequate vegetative cover to control erosion; periodically inspect and repair runoff water outlets

records.name: Cross Wind Ridges
records.problem: Wind erosion; reduced plant productivity and health; particulate matter emissions
records.strategies: Ridges formed by tillage, planting, or other operations and aligned perpendicular to prevailing wind direction during critical wind erosion periods; ridges may be established using chisel plows, drills with hoe openers, or other implements that form effective ridges
records.eligibility: Applies to cropland with soils stable enough to sustain effective ridges and cloddiness, such as loamy and clayey soil materials; not well adapted to sandy soils and certain organic soils
records.requirements: Ridge orientation, height, spacing, and period of use must be designed using approved wind erosion prediction technology; ridge orientation during critical erosion periods must not exceed 45° from perpendicular to erosive wind direction; spacing between ridges must be no more than four times ridge height; ridges must be maintained during periods when wind erosion is expected or until crops provide sufficient protective cover
records.notes: May help reduce wind erosion where SWI-related vegetation loss leaves soil exposed.

records.name: Dam
records.problem: Downstream flood damage; insufficient water storage; degraded fish and wildlife habitat
records.strategies: Artificial barrier used to impound water; may provide flood-control storage and permanent water storage for beneficial uses such as irrigation or livestock supply; may include shallow reservoir areas and wetland habitat for wildlife
records.eligibility: Site must have satisfactory topographic, geologic, hydrologic, and soil conditions; upstream conservation practices must sufficiently control sediment yield; sufficient quantity and quality of water must be available without impairing downstream or adjacent uses or functions
records.requirements: Must comply with applicable Federal, Tribal, State, and local requirements and obtain required permits; dam hazard classification and appropriate design criteria are required; principal and auxiliary spillways must be provided as applicable; disturbed areas must be stabilized; plans/specifications and an operation and maintenance plan are required

records.name: Precision Land Forming and Smoothing
records.problem: Poor surface drainage; erosion; surface irregularities that interfere with drainage and equipment operation
records.strategies: Regrading fields to remove depressions, mounds, old terraces, turnrows, and other surface irregularities; developing uniform slopes to allow drainage across the field; balancing cuts and fills; carrying runoff to a stable outlet
records.eligibility: Applies to fields where depressions, mounds, old terraces, turnrows, and other surface irregularities interfere with or adversely affect surface drainage, erosion control, and equipment operation; does not apply to land leveling for irrigation
records.requirements: Requires engineering surveys and investigations; grading plan with uniform slopes and acceptable grades; drainage practices to handle runoff without excessive erosion and carry runoff to a stable outlet; soil must have sufficient depth and suitable texture for the planned land use; written O&M plan with annual and post-storm inspections

records.name: Roots for Resilience - Living Shoreline
records.problem: Shoreline erosion, tidal marsh loss, wetland degradation, conversion of marsh to open water, and sea-level rise impacts
records.eligibility: Applications may be submitted by local jurisdictions, nonprofit organizations, and institutions of higher education. Projects must be located within the Chesapeake Bay portions of Dorchester, Somerset, or Wicomico Counties. Projects on public lands are preferred, but projects on private lands are also eligible with documented landowner support
records.requirements: Protect high-quality tidal marsh habitat at risk of conversion to open water; incorporate sea level rise into project design; provide landowner permission; demonstrate long-term project success.
records.practice: Living Shoreline Restoration and Marsh Protection
records.strategies: Fiber coir logs, sills, groins, breakwaters, sand, marsh plantings, and other natural materials used to protect, restore, enhance, or create shoreline habitat

records.name: Roots for Resilience - Enhanced Forestry Management and Afforestation Projects
records.problem: Climate change impacts affecting forests and communities, including sea level rise, saltwater intrusion, ghost forests, wetland migration, extreme heat, and storms.
records.county: Caroline, Dorchester, Talbot, Somerset, Wicomico, Worcester
records.requirements: Support implementation of 500 acres of afforestation and 1,000 acres of enhanced forest management on public and private lands in Caroline, Dorchester, Somerset, Talbot, Wicomico, and Worcester Counties. Forest management projects are selected and planned by the Maryland Forest Service and implemented through direct on-the-ground management activities
records.practice: Afforestation; Enhanced Forest Management
records.strategies: Afforestation dominated by Atlantic white-cedar, baldcypress, and shortleaf pine; reforestation; crop tree release; pre-commercial thinning; invasive species control; aerial herbicide treatments; and prescribed burning associated with forest management objectives

records.name: Maryland Agricultural Cost-Share Program (MACS)
records.problem: Nutrient runoff, sediment loss, poor drainage, flooding, erosion, degraded water quality, agricultural impacts to surface and groundwater
records.eligibility: Applicants may be farm owners, landlords, tenants, partnerships, corporations, trusts, or other business entities involved in farm operations. Practices must address existing or potential agricultural nonpoint source pollution from cropland, pastureland, hay land, livestock, or poultry operations. Projects must be located on a farm
records.requirements: Must address an existing or potential agricultural nonpoint source pollution problem, meet BMP-specific eligibility criteria, comply with Nutrient Management requirements, and maintain installed practices according to approved operation and maintenance plans
records.practice: Supports implementation of more than 41 agricultural best management practices (BMPs) that address erosion, nutrients, animal waste, agricultural chemicals, drainage, and water quality concerns
records.notes: Applications are accepted through local Soil Conservation Districts. Farmers should contact their local district to apply and determine eligibility for specific BMP

records.name: Shoreline Erosion Loan Program
records.problem: Shoreline erosion, marsh loss, coastal flooding, sea-level rise impacts
records.eligibility: Individuals or groups of homeowners, non-profit organizations, community organizations, counties and municipalities
records.practiceWebsite: Develop living shorelines to reduce erosion and marsh loss
records.strategies: Nature-based shoreline stabilization using marsh vegetation, sand, oyster reefs, coir logs, and other natural materials to reduce erosion and protect wetland

records.name: Conservation Reserve Enhancement Permanent Easement Program (CREP)
records.problem: Nutrient and sediment runoff, loss of riparian protection, highly erodible land, wetland degradation, wildlife habitat loss, and increased vulnerability to coastal flooding and climate impact
records.eligibility: Must have an existing CREP or CRP contract and have installed approved conservation practices. Eligible lands include cropland adjacent to streams and water bodies, highly erodible cropland within 1,000 feet of a stream, and certain pasturelands adjacent to streams.
records.requirements: Landowner must maintain approved conservation practices according to the conservation plan or forest stewardship plan, control noxious and invasive weeds, and comply with maintenance and monitoring requirements. Easement participants must maintain practices in perpetuity
records.practice: Riparian Forest Buffer (CP22); Filter Strip (CP21); Wildlife Habitat Buffer (CP4D); Marginal Pastureland Wildlife Buffer (CP29); Marginal Pastureland Wetland Buffer (CP30); Native Grasses (CP2); Introduced Grasses/Legumes (CP1); Softwood Trees (CP3); Hardwood Trees (CP3A); Shallow Water Area for Wildlife (CP9); Wetland Restoration (CP23, CP23A); Habitat for Declining Species (CP25).
records.strategies: Riparian buffers, filter strips, wildlife habitat buffers, wetland restoration, wetland buffers, native grass plantings, tree plantings, shallow water habitat, and habitat for declining species
records.notes: https://dnr.maryland.gov/wildlife/Documents/CREP_Start-to-Finish.pdf

records.name: Maryland Forest Legacy Program
records.problem: Forest loss, forest fragmentation, development pressure, loss of wildlife habitat, declining water quality, and loss of forest resilience to climate impacts
records.eligibility: Only private forestland located within a designated Forest Legacy Area is eligible. At least 75% of the property proposed for easement must be forested; up to 25% may be in compatible uses such as agriculture
records.requirements: Participation is voluntary ("willing seller–willing buyer"). Properties are evaluated and ranked based on forest importance, threat of conversion, and conservation value. A Forest Stewardship Plan is required before project completion and must be updated periodically
records.practice: Permanent Conservation Easement; Forest Stewardship Plan Implementation; Sustainable Forest Management; Forest Conservation and Protection from Development

records.name: Coastal Resilience Program
records.problem: High tide flooding, storm surge, sea level rise, erosion, flooding, coastal hazards, and long-term climate impacts affecting coastal communities, infrastructure, and natural resources.
records.eligibility: Communities seeking technical assistance, financial assistance, training, planning resources, and resilience support through the Chesapeake & Coastal Grants Gateway. Public and private lands are eligible, but projects on private lands must demonstrate a community-wide benefit and provide an access/landowner agreement.

records.name: Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation (MALPF)
records.problem: Farmland conversion, farmland fragmentation, loss of productive agricultural and forest land, development pressure
records.eligibility: Land must be used for producing food or fiber or have the capability to do so. Minimum property size is generally 50 contiguous acres (exceptions may apply). Property must meet soil productivity criteria and generally be located outside a 10-year water and sewer service area. A soil conservation and water quality plan is required; properties with more than 25 acres of contiguous forest must also have a Forest Stewardship Plan. Eligibility- County Government, Individuals, Municipalities/Towns, Non-Profit, Regional
records.requirements: Landowner voluntarily sells a permanent agricultural preservation easement that restricts future residential, commercial, and industrial development. Soil conservation and water quality practices identified in the approved plan must be implemented. Properties with ≥25 acres of contiguous forest must maintain a Forest Stewardship Plan.
records.practice: Agricultural Preservation Easement Acquisition

records.name: Maryland’s Rural Legacy Program
records.problem: Degraded water quality; wetland degradation; degraded wildlife habitat; loss of agricultural and forest lands
records.eligibility: Property must be located within a designated Rural Legacy Area (RLA), defined as a region rich in agricultural, natural, forestry, and cultural resources. Sponsors may be local governments, land trusts, or co-sponsors
records.requirements: Sponsors must submit an application, develop a Rural Legacy Plan, document public participation, develop partnerships, prepare a monitoring protocol, and provide long-term stewardship, monitoring, and enforcement of conservation easements.
records.practice: Conservation Easement Purchase; Fee Simple Purchase; Fee Simple Purchase and Resale with Conservation Easement; Donation of Easement or Fee Simple Interest
records.strategies: Conservation easements are perpetual and protect agricultural, forestry, natural, scenic, and cultural resources. Easements may include soil conservation plans, water quality plans, forest management plans, riparian buffers, development-right limitations, subdivision restrictions, residential density limits, habitat protection areas, and other resource protection measures.

records.name: Maryland Conservation Buffer Initiative
records.problem: Poor infiltration; nutrient-related water quality degradation; soil erosion; degraded water quality
records.eligibility: Farmers and landowners responsible for managing eligible lands may apply. Eligible lands include cropland adjacent to streams or ditches with an established cropping history in pasture, commodity crops, or hay, and areas adjacent to watercourses with highly erodible or hydric soils. Farmers leasing land must certify an active lease or provide landowner approval. Applicants must be in good standing with USDA and state cost-share programs and submit a current Nutrient Management Plan Certification. Existing buffers and lands enrolled in state or federal conservation programs or required by easements are not eligible.
records.requirements: Applications are accepted on a first-come, first-served basis through local Soil Conservation Districts. Applicants must submit a map showing the buffer location and acreage, a signed Nutrient Management Plan Certification Form, and a signed IRS Form W-9. Buffers must be planted within one year of the signed agreement. Contracts are for 5 or 10 years. Nutrient applications are prohibited on enrolled buffer areas.
records.practice: Conservation Buffers
records.strategies: Eligible practices include: (1) Grass Buffers on Watercourses, ranging from 10–100 ft wide; (2) Forest Buffers on Watercourses planted with trees and shrubs, ranging from 35–100 ft wide; and (3) Watercourse Access Control Areas adjacent to livestock pastures, ranging from 10–100 ft wide and requiring a minimum width of 35 ft when woody vegetation is established. No grazing is allowed within access control areas. Field ditches are not eligible for woody conservation buffers. Riparian forest buffer projects may include pasture fencing.
records.notes: Payment rates range from $500/acre for existing grass buffers to $4,500/acre for riparian forest buffers with pasture fencing. Participants receive 75% of project costs up front and 25% after planting verification. Additional tree bonus payments and annual maintenance payments for up to five years are available for forest buffers. Free technical assistance is provided through local Soil Conservation Districts.

records.name: Whole Watershed Program (WWP)
records.problem: Nutrient runoff; degraded water quality; flooding; wetland degradation; salt marsh deterioration
records.agency: Maryland Department of Natural Resources (DNR) in partnership with MDA, MDE, and other state agencies
records.eligibility: Municipal, county, and regional agencies; nonprofit organizations; faith-based organizations; homeowners associations; and soil/water conservation districts may apply. A single Project Sponsor must be identified to administer the project
records.requirements: Projects must occur within an approved watershed and demonstrate benefits for water quality, habitat restoration, environmental justice, climate resilience, and community engagement. Project Sponsors must provide at least 50% matching implementation funding, hold at least four community meetings annually, and participate in regular coordination with the State Management Team
records.practice: Watershed Restoration and Conservation
records.strategies: Eligible actions may include wetland restoration, riparian forest buffers, stream restoration, shoreline stabilization, living shorelines, stormwater management, afforestation, habitat restoration, septic remediation, wastewater improvements, agricultural conservation practices, cattle exclusion fencing, row crop conversion to pasture, and other watershed-scale restoration activities
records.notes: Five-year pilot program established through the Whole Watershed Act (2024). Selected watersheds receive long-term technical and financial support. The program funds up to 50% of implementation costs and emphasizes measurable outcomes, watershed-scale planning, community engagement, pollution reduction, habitat creation, carbon sequestration, climate resilience, and public access improvement

records.name: Maryland Cover Crop Program
records.problem: Poor aggregate stability; poor infiltration; nutrient runoff; soil erosion; reduced soil health/organic matter; poor soil moisture efficiency
records.eligibility: Applicants must be in good standing with the Conservation Grants Program and in compliance with Maryland nutrient management requirements. A minimum of 10 acres of cover crops must be planted. Enrolled acreage cannot exceed acreage listed in the Nutrient Management Plan.
records.requirements: Applicants must submit a Nutrient Management Plan Certification and IRS Form W-9. Cover crops must be planted following program deadlines, certified with the local Soil Conservation District within one week of planting and by November 12, 2026, and all follow-up documentation must be submitted by December 1, 2026. Additional restrictions may apply.
records.practice: Cover Crops
records.strategies: cover crops may be planted after corn, soybeans, sorghum, tobacco, vegetables, hemp, sunflowers, sod, or millet. Eligible species include cereal grains (wheat/spelt, rye, barley, triticale, oats, ryegrass), brassicas (forage radish, canola/rape), and legumes (clover, Austrian winter peas, hairy vetch). Multi-species mixes are encouraged. Cover crops may be grazed or harvested for on-farm livestock forage after establishment. Non-poultry manure applications are permitted under specific conditions.c

records.name: Maryland Cover Crop Plus Program
records.problem: Poor aggregate stability; poor infiltration; reduced soil health/organic matter; poor soil moisture efficiency; nutrient runoff
records.eligibility: Applicants must be in good standing with the Maryland Nutrient Management Program, Maryland Agricultural Water Quality Cost-Share Program, Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation Program, and other MDA conservation grant programs. A current Nutrient Management Plan Certification Form is required. Enrollment is limited to 10–500 acres.
records.requirements: Participants must sign a 3-year contract and submit a 3-year management plan. At least two of the three years must include cover crop scenarios not supported by traditional MDA cover crop programs. Field maps are required. Grazing plans are required for grazing scenarios. A letter of support is required when working with a Technical Service Provider (TSP). Cover crops must generally be planted by November 1 and terminated no earlier than April 15 unless an approved alternative scenario applies.
records.practice: Cover Crops
records.strategies: Eligible practices include summer cover crops, cover crop mixes containing less than 50% grasses, legumes managed for nitrogen production, cover crops planted into standing crops before August 1, interseeded cover crops in wide crop rows, early termination of grass-legume mixtures, and cover crops managed for adaptive/rotational grazing. Alternative cover crop strategies supported by approved Technical Service Providers may also qualify. Seeding rates and species mixtures must follow NRCS technical guidelines unless approved alternatives are provided.

Annapolis, MD 21401
records.notes: Base payment is $40/acre. Additional bonuses are available for diversity, summer cover crops, biomass production, and fertilizer reduction. Maximum payments may reach $100/acre. Diversity bonuses require at least three species from three functional groups. Biomass bonuses require at least 2,000 lb/acre of biomass. Nitrogen reduction bonuses require documentation of at least a 15% reduction in commercial fertilizer use from the previous year's baseline.

records.name: MD Healthy Soils
records.problem: Poor aggregate stability; poor infiltration; reduced soil health/organic matter; poor soil moisture efficiency; nutrient runoff; degraded wildlife habitat
records.eligibility: Open to individual farmers, groups of farmers, and individuals or organizations working with farmers in Maryland. Participating farms must have a gross annual income of at least $2,500 (or $2,500 in donated agricultural products for nonprofit entities) and/or manage 8 or more animal units (8,000 pounds of live animal weight). Applicants must provide a Current Nutrient Management Plan Certification demonstrating compliance with Maryland nutrient management requirements. There are no minimum or maximum acreage requirements.
records.requirements: Applicants submit a competitive grant application including a project narrative, budget, field maps, recent soil tests, and supporting templates as applicable. records.name: Maryland Environmental Trust (MET)
records.problem: Loss of farmland, forest fragmentation, wetland loss, loss of wildlife habitat, degradation of riparian buffers, and development pressure
records.eligibility: Properties must provide significant public conservation benefit through protection of natural habitat, open space (including farmland and forest land), historic resources, or outdoor recreation and education. MET gives preference to productive farmland, significant woodlands, wetlands, wildlife habitat, riparian buffers, and conservation corridors. Rural properties are generally expected to be at least 25 acres.
records.requirements: Landowners voluntarily donate a perpetual conservation easement. Owners retain ownership and management responsibilities while permanently protecting conservation attributes. MET conducts annual monitoring and enforcement of easement terms.
records.practice: Conservation Easement
records.strategies: Conservation easements are perpetual agreements that bind all present and future landowners. The landowner retains ownership of the property while giving up certain property rights, including the right to develop, subdivide the land, and mine gravel. Easements may allow continued agricultural activities, construction of farm buildings, modifications to existing homes, and other uses specified in the easement.
records.notes: Easements are perpetual and recorded in local land records. The public does not automatically gain access to the property. The land may be sold, but the easement remains attached to the property and binds future owners. Requests for easement donations may be submitted at any time. Potential tax deductions and estate tax benefits may be available to landowners who donate easements.

records.practice: Tree planting; afforestation; selected reforestation; invasive species removal/control; prescribed fire; site preparation; post-planting maintenance; tree shelters; burn plans/fire breaks
records.strategies: Eligible reforestation can include oak species, shortleaf pine, Atlantic white cedar, bald cypress, and pitch pine; afforestation uses native species other than loblolly pine; all species must be site-appropriate.
records.costShare: Cost-share: most payments at 90%; 100% for certain landowners/properties (owned forestland 10 years or less, priority areas, limited resource producers, or qualifying veterans). Prescribed fire and invasive species projects capped at $10,000 per landowner; tree planting has no maximum payment listed.
records.benefit: Reimbursement for prescribed fire/invasive species after verified implementation; tree-planting payments made directly to suppliers/contractors.
records.limitations: May not directly address saline soils or hydrology
records.quantitative: Funding pool: $1.5 million. Minimum project size: 3 acres. Typical cost-share: 90%; possible 100%; $10,000 cap for prescribed fire/invasive species; no listed maximum for tree planting.

records.name: Forest Stewardship Program / Free Forest Management Plans

records.limitations: Permanent restriction may reduce future flexibility if land is actively converting due to SWI or marsh migration. Does not itself fund hydrologic restoration or salinity management.
records.quantitative: Perpetual easement. Payment specifics depend on appraisal/easement acquisition.

records.eligibility:
Applications for cost-share assistance must be submitted for each practice and are approved on a first-come first-served basis. A signed Cooperators Agreement will be required for each applicant.

All practices must meet or exceed USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) standards and must be maintained for a period of ten years. No cost-share will be provided for standards that are considered to be optional and are not necessary for the practice to be constructed to meet NRCS specifications.

A Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) Lien will be filed with the Kent County Recorder of Deeds for all conservation practices with the exception of drainage practices. The nonrefundable filing fee of $61 is the responsibility of the applicant and must be submitted with the cost-share application. Likewise, at the end of the maintenance agreement period, the fee to remove the lien will be the responsibility of the property owner at that time.
